mainTopic: Whether 'שור או כשב' excludes כלאים from קרבנות, and where רבא's rule that 'שה' excludes כלאים is actually needed
overview: The גמרא keeps working on the פסוק about animals fit for קרבנות (ויקרא 22:27: 'שור או כשב או עז'). It asks why 'שור או כשב' should not include כלאים. It answers that both halves of the פסוק exclude: one excludes כלאים and the other excludes a נדמה. Two inclusions would make no sense, but two exclusions do. Then the גמרא asks what רבא's rule, that 'שה' always excludes כלאים, is needed for. קדשים, מעשר בהמה and בכור all have their own sources, so the rule must be for פטר חמור, which may not be redeemed with כלאים. But רבי אלעזר allows redeeming with כלאים. For him, the rule teaches that an animal born from a kosher mother and a non-kosher father is not kosher. This answer works only if we do not follow רבי יהושע. The amud ends as the גמרא begins proving that a kosher animal can become pregnant from a non-kosher one, and that proof continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Why not include mixed breeds for sacrifices too?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: the פסוק of קדשים also says 'שור או כשב', two animals that cannot produce כלאים together, so let it include כלאים.
steps.simpleTranslation: But for sacrificial animals the Torah also says 'a bull or a sheep,' two animals that cannot produce a mixed breed together. So let us include a mixed-breed animal!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא takes the same kind of reasoning it used before and applies it to the פסוק about קרבנות. It asks why this פסוק should not also include כלאים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A bull and a sheep cannot mate to produce a mixed animal, so naming them together seems to point toward including כלאים. If that logic works elsewhere, it should work here too. That would make an animal of כלאים fit for the מזבח.

keyTerms.meaning: Sacrificial animals, animals set aside for the Temple
A mixed breed, an animal born from two different species
'A bull or a sheep', the opening words of ויקרא 22:27
'So let us include'

phrases.english: But regarding sacrificial animals it is also stated:
"A bull or a sheep"

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵין אַתָּה יָכוֹל לְהוֹצִיא כִּלְאַיִם מִבֵּינֵיהֶם,
phrases.english: from which you cannot produce a mixed breed between them,
so let us include [a mixed breed]!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the reasoning from the earlier discussion to the פסוק of קדשים.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading of 'שור או כשב' in ויקרא 22:27 as excluding כלאים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If naming two species that cannot interbreed points to including כלאים, the same should hold for the פסוק about קרבנות.

steps.title: The end of the verse excludes, so the beginning excludes too
steps.stepSummary: Since the end of the פסוק ('או עז') clearly comes to exclude, the beginning ('שור או כשב') must also come to exclude.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since the end of the verse comes to exclude, the beginning of the verse also comes to exclude.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by reading the whole פסוק together. The end of the פסוק excludes something, so the beginning should be read the same way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The end clause 'או עז' is understood as excluding a נדמה, an animal that looks like a different species. The גמרא reads both halves of the פסוק as working the same way. So 'שור או כשב' excludes כלאים rather than including it.

keyTerms.meaning: The end part of a פסוק or teaching
The first part of a פסוק or teaching
To exclude

phrases.english: Since the end clause comes to exclude,
phrases.notes: The end clause is 'או עז', 'or a goat', which leaves out an animal that looks like another species.

phrases.english: the first clause also comes to exclude.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading the parts of the פסוק as consistent with each other
steps.terutzMaskana: Both halves of the פסוק exclude, so 'שור או כשב' excludes כלאים.

steps.title: Maybe both parts of the verse include instead
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא flips the argument: maybe the first part includes, so the end part should also include.
steps.simpleTranslation: On the contrary! Since the first part comes to include, the end part should also come to include!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer by flipping it. If the two halves must match, why not say both include?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in step 2 relied on the halves of the פסוק matching. That same idea could work in the other direction. So the challenge says the end clause should include just like the beginning.

keyTerms.meaning: On the contrary, the opposite is true
To include

phrases.english: On the contrary: since the first clause comes to include,
the end clause also comes to include!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the logic of step 2 around.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in step 2 that both halves exclude
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The idea that the halves must match works just as well for including as for excluding.

steps.title: Two exclusions make sense, two inclusions do not
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the flipped argument. Two exclusions are both needed, but two inclusions would be pointless, because once כלאים is included a נדמה is obviously included.
steps.simpleTranslation: What kind of comparison is this? If you say both parts exclude, it makes sense that two exclusions were needed: even after a mixed breed was excluded, the Torah still had to exclude a look-alike. But if you say they include, why two inclusions? Once a mixed breed is included, is there any question about a look-alike?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the 'on the contrary' argument. It shows that only the excluding reading gives each half of the פסוק a job.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A נדמה is born from parents of one species, so it is easier to accept than a mixed breed. If the Torah excluded כלאים, we might still think a נדמה is fine, so a second exclusion is needed. If the Torah included כלאים, a נדמה would surely be included too, so a second inclusion would add nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: 'What is this?', meaning the comparison does not work
An animal that looks like a different species from its mother
Exclusions
Inclusions
'Is it even a question?'

steps.whatToRemember: In ויקרא 22:27, 'שור או כשב' excludes כלאים and 'או עז' excludes a נדמה. Only the excluding reading gives both halves of the פסוק a job.
steps.confusionAlert: The argument works because a נדמה is the easier case: its parents are one species. A mixed breed is the harder case. So excluding the harder case does not exclude the easier one automatically, but including the harder case does include the easier one automatically.

phrases.english: What is this [comparison]?
Granted, if you say [both] come to exclude,
that is why two exclusions were needed;
for even though a mixed breed was excluded,
it was necessary to exclude a look-alike.
But if you say [they] come to include,
why are two inclusions needed?
Now that a mixed breed is included,
is a look-alike even a question?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the flipped argument of step 3 and confirms step 2.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The suggestion that both halves of the פסוק include
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Two inclusions would be pointless, since including כלאים already includes a נדמה.

steps.title: What הלכה is רבא's 'שה' rule for?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא now questions רבא's rule that wherever 'שה' appears it excludes כלאים, and asks which halacha the rule is needed for.
steps.simpleTranslation: But what about what רבא said: 'This established a paradigm: wherever the Torah says "שה," it comes only to exclude a mixed breed.' For what הלכה did he need this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new challenge against רבא's general rule. It asks where that rule is actually needed, and the next steps go through the possible answers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The discussion so far has treated 'שה' in the theft laws as not excluding כלאים, which already raises a question about רבא's rule. Now the גמרא asks a sharper question: which halacha would ever need the rule at all? If every possible case already has its own source, the rule seems to have no purpose.

keyTerms.meaning: 'This built a father', a source that sets a pattern for other places
A sheep or goat, a word for a small animal of the flock
'For what halacha?', meaning where is this rule needed

phrases.english: But this that רבא said:
phrases.notes: 'But' here means: if 'שה' in the theft laws doesn't exclude mixed breeds, what is רבא's rule for?

phrases.english: This established a paradigm:
wherever "seh" is stated,
it comes only to exclude a mixed breed;
for what halacha?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the פסוק of קדשים to questioning רבא's general rule.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's rule that 'שה' always excludes כלאים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If every halacha that might need the rule already has its own source, the rule has no use.

steps.title: Not needed for sacrifices
steps.stepSummary: The rule cannot be for קדשים, because 'שור או כשב' already excludes כלאים there explicitly.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it is for sacrificial animals, it is written explicitly about them: 'a bull or a sheep,' which excludes a mixed breed!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the first possible use of רבא's rule and rules it out. קרבנות already have their own source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 2 through 4 showed that 'שור או כשב' excludes כלאים from the מזבח. So the rule about 'שה' adds nothing for קדשים.

keyTerms.meaning: Explicitly, openly
'Except for', excluding

phrases.english: If for sacrificial animals,
it is explicitly written about them:
"a bull or a sheep" – excluding a mixed breed!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the first possible answer to 'for what halacha?'.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: קדשים already has an explicit source excluding כלאים.

steps.title: Not needed for animal tithe either
steps.stepSummary: The rule cannot be for מעשר בהמה either, because a גזירה שוה of 'תחת' and 'תחת' teaches it from קדשים.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it is for animal tithe, that is learned from the word 'under' here and 'under' there, from sacrificial animals!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rules out the second possible use of רבא's rule. מעשר בהמה learns from קדשים, which already excludes כלאים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק of מעשר בהמה says 'תחת השבט' and the פסוק of קדשים says 'תחת אמו'. Because the same word appears in both, מעשר learns from קדשים, so כלאים is excluded there too. Once again רבא's rule seems unnecessary. Step 10 finally finds where it is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: Here, מעשר בהמה, the tithe of every tenth animal
'Under', the shared word used for the comparison
He learns, he derives

phrases.english: If for animal tithe,
he derives "under" and "under" from sacrificial animals!
phrases.notes: The same word appears in ויקרא 27:32 (tithe) and ויקרא 22:27 (sacrifices), so the two laws are linked.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי לְמַעֲשֵׂר תַּחַת תַּחַת יָלֵיף מִקֳּדָשִׁים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the second possible answer to 'for what halacha?'.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Using רבא's rule for מעשר בהמה
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: מעשר בהמה already learns the exclusion of כלאים from קדשים through the shared word 'תחת'.

steps.title: The rule is not needed for a firstborn animal
steps.stepSummary: רבא's rule cannot be for בכור, because a גזירה שוה of 'העברה' and 'העברה' teaches it from מעשר בהמה.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say the rule is for a firstborn animal, that is also already known. We learn it from animal tithe through the matching word 'passing' that appears in both places.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a third possible use for רבא's rule, the laws of בכור, and pushes it away too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 7 we saw that מעשר בהמה learns from קדשים that כלאים is excluded. Now בכור learns from מעשר through the shared word 'העברה'. So the exclusion of כלאים from בכור is already covered, and רבא's rule adds nothing here.

keyTerms.meaning: A firstborn animal, which is holy
'Passing', a word used both for בכור and for מעשר
He learns it, meaning it is derived

phrases.english: If it is for a firstborn animal,
it is learned from 'passing' and 'passing',
phrases.notes: שמות 13:12 uses 'pass' for בכור, and ויקרא 27:32 uses 'passes under the rod' for מעשר.

phrases.english: from animal tithe!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the series of rejections: after קדשים and מעשר, now בכור.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rules out בכור as the place where רבא's rule is needed.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The exclusion of כלאים from בכור is already taught by a גזירה שוה from מעשר, which itself learns from קדשים.

steps.title: A second reason the rule is not needed for a firstborn
steps.stepSummary: Another reason: the פסוק excludes a נדמה from בכור, so a כלאים is certainly excluded.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or another way: you agree that an animal that looks like a different species is not a firstborn, because the verse says 'the firstborn of an ox', meaning the mother is an ox and its firstborn is an ox. If so, do we even need a verse to exclude a mixed breed?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, separate reason why רבא's rule is not needed for בכור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק requires the mother and the baby to be the same kind, so a נדמה, which looks different from its mother, is not a בכור. A כלאים is even further from its parent, so it is obviously excluded. This is the same logic as step 4: once one case is excluded, the more obvious case needs no extra source.

keyTerms.meaning: Alternatively, another way to answer
An animal that looks like a different species than its mother
Is it needed? Meaning: obviously not

phrases.english: Alternatively, you say a look-alike is not a firstborn,
as it is written: 'But the firstborn of an ox',
only when it, the mother, is an ox
and its firstborn is an ox;
is a mixed breed even a question?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different reason for the same rejection made in step 8.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Again rules out בכור as the use of רבא's rule.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: If a נדמה is excluded by the פסוק, then כלאים is excluded all the more, so no separate rule is needed.

steps.title: The rule is needed for redeeming a firstborn donkey
steps.stepSummary: רבא's rule was said about פטר חמור: the משנה says one may not redeem it with כלאים, and the rule supplies the source.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא's rule was said about redeeming a firstborn donkey. As the משנה teaches: you may not redeem it with a calf, a wild animal, a slaughtered animal, a טריפה, a mixed breed, or a כוי.
steps.whatsHappening: After ruling out קדשים, מעשר and בכור, the גמרא finally finds where רבא's rule is needed: פטר חמור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A firstborn donkey is redeemed with a 'שה'. The משנה lists animals that do not count, including כלאים. רבא's rule, that 'שה' excludes כלאים, is the source for that line of the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: A firstborn donkey, which must be redeemed with a שה
Redeem
An animal with a fatal injury or defect
An animal whose kind is uncertain, possibly wild and possibly domestic

phrases.english: Rather, when רבא's rule was stated,
it was about a firstborn donkey.
As we learned in a משנה: one may not redeem it
not with a calf, nor with a wild animal,
nor with a slaughtered animal, nor with a טריפה,
nor with a mixed breed, nor with a כוי.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After all the rejections, gives the real answer to the question of step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Finds a new area where the rule is needed
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It seemed רבא's rule had no use, since every case was already covered by another source.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule teaches that a firstborn donkey may not be redeemed with כלאים.
steps.whatToRemember: רבא's rule, 'wherever שה appears it excludes כלאים', is needed for פטר חמור, not for קדשים, מעשר or בכור.

steps.title: What is the rule for according to רבי אלעזר?
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר allows redeeming a פטר חמור with כלאים because it is a שה. So for him, what is רבא's rule needed for?
steps.simpleTranslation: But according to רבי אלעזר, who allows a mixed breed, as the משנה says: 'רבי אלעזר allows a mixed breed because it is a שה', what halacha is the rule for?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer of step 10: it works only for the first opinion in the משנה, not for רבי אלעזר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר holds that כלאים is a שה and can be used to redeem a donkey. So for him, פטר חמור cannot be where 'שה' excludes כלאים. The search for the rule's purpose opens again.

keyTerms.meaning: Permits
A sheep or goat
For what halacha? What is it needed for?

phrases.english: But according to רבי אלעזר, who permits a mixed breed,
as we learned: רבי אלעזר permits a mixed breed
because it is a שה,
for what halacha is the rule needed?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 10 using רבי אלעזר's opinion in the same משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that רבא's rule is for פטר חמור.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי אלעזר counts כלאים as a שה for פטר חמור, so the rule cannot apply there for him, and it still needs a purpose.
steps.confusionAlert: רבי אלעזר is not arguing with רבא directly. He argues in the משנה about פטר חמור, and that removes the only use the גמרא had found for רבא's rule.

steps.title: For רבי אלעזר, the rule teaches that a mixed animal born from a kosher mother is not kosher
steps.stepSummary: On behalf of רבי אלעזר, the גמרא answers that רבא's rule was said about an animal born from a kosher mother but conceived from a non-kosher father. Such an animal is not kosher. This answer does not follow רבי יהושע, who learns that law from 'שה כשבים ושה עזים'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר can tell you: רבא's rule was said about a non-kosher animal that was born from a kosher mother and conceived from a non-kosher father. This does not follow רבי יהושע. רבי יהושע learns this law from the words 'the שה of sheep and the שה of goats,' which teach that the animal is kosher only if its father is a sheep and its mother is a ewe.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 11. Even for רבי אלעזר, it finds a job for רבא's rule: it teaches that an animal born from a kosher mother and a non-kosher father may not be eaten.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's rule says that 'שה' excludes כלאים. The rule now moves to the פסוק about which animals are kosher, where 'שה' teaches that this mixed offspring is not kosher. רבי יהושע already learns this from the doubled wording 'שה כשבים ושה עזים', so the answer only works if we do not follow רבי יהושע.

keyTerms.meaning: A non-kosher animal born from a kosher mother
Its conception, meaning the father that made the mother pregnant
'The שה of sheep and the שה of goats', the פסוק listing kosher animals

steps.whyThisMatters: The rule now does a different job: it decides כשרות instead of redemption. That is how רבי אלעזר can still use רבא's rule.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 11's question about what רבא's rule is needed for according to רבי אלעזר.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Moves the rule to a different case (kashrus of a mixed offspring)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since רבי אלעזר allows redeeming a פטר חמור with כלאים, it seemed that רבא's rule has no use for him.
steps.terutzMaskana: For רבי אלעזר, רבא's rule teaches that an animal from a kosher mother and a non-kosher father is not kosher. This holds only if we do not follow רבי יהושע.

steps.title: Can a kosher animal become pregnant from a non-kosher one?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the case is even possible: can a kosher animal become pregnant from a non-kosher animal?
steps.simpleTranslation: Can a kosher animal really become pregnant from a non-kosher one?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops to check whether the case from step 12 can happen at all. If it cannot, there would be no need for a פסוק to teach it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both רבא's rule, as just explained, and רבי יהושע's פסוק are about this mixed offspring. If a kosher animal can never become pregnant from a non-kosher one, those sources would be teaching about a case that never happens.

keyTerms.meaning: A kosher female animal
Becomes pregnant

phrases.english: But can a kosher animal become pregnant from a non-kosher one?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions whether the case used in step 12's answer can really happen.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether it is physically possible for a kosher animal to become pregnant from a non-kosher animal.

steps.title: Yes, it is possible, and the גמרא begins bringing a source
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers yes, and starts to bring a known source to show that it can happen.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says yes, a kosher animal can become pregnant from a non-kosher one. It is setting up a source that proves this, and the proof continues in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer 'yes' keeps the case from step 12 in place. The words 'דקיימא לן' tell us an accepted principle is about to be quoted as proof.
